## TL;DR

Addressed the review coverage gap with a second headless QA pass. Confirmed the empty Deployments setup state through an exact API interception made before fresh navigation. Confirmed that opening Context > Discover triggers the curated catalog request, which returned HTTP 200 and populated results within 60 seconds. Updated the QA record with those outcomes and the corrected test method. No reproducible application bug was found, so no source fix or regression test was needed.

## Work and rationale

The first review correctly noted that the recorded evidence did not prove an empty Deployments state and left Discover unresolved in its loading state. I checked the task state and confirmed it had returned to active for the review fix. I then started the auth-less preview server from the assigned task worktree and kept all browser work in Playwright Chromium headless mode.

For Deployments, I inspected the page loader. It uses the page-data cache, so a route interception that does not match the request before fresh navigation can leave already loaded data visible. I opened a fresh page, registered an exact `**/api/deployments` interception before navigating, and captured request and response events. The trace showed a request to `http://127.0.0.1:7272/api/deployments`, the route interception, and a 200 response. The fixture represented a disabled, empty deployment setup (`enabled: false`, empty rows and branches). The page then displayed its expected guidance: deployments are not configured and a `[[deployments]]` block is needed. At 375px its document width remained 375px. This proves the missing state that the original pass had not established.

For Discover, my previous direct `?tab=discover` visit did not exercise the catalog load path. Inspection showed the request is started by a watcher when the user changes the selected tab to Discover; the initial query value does not invoke that watcher. I repeated the check from the Docs tab by clicking the Discover button and attached request, response, failed-request, console-error, and page-error listeners. The browser recorded a request to `/api/skill-registry/curated` and an HTTP 200 response. After waiting 60 seconds, the loading message was gone and catalog entries were visible, including skills with publishers and install counts. No console or page errors and no failed catalog request were recorded. The check therefore verifies normal completion after the actual user action, rather than inferring success from the route alone.

I updated `docs/qa/2026-11-deployments-dev-context.md` to record both observations, the request evidence, viewport behavior, and why the initial probes were inconclusive. The previous populated Deployments, Dev, Docs, mobile layout, and safe-control observations remain documented. The task's external-action boundary also remains: I did not confirm a deployment push or start a configured dev command.

## Approaches tried

The initial empty Deployments check had matched a broad pattern but did not replace the cached data shown in that run. I replaced it with a fresh browser page, exact endpoint interception, and explicit request/response trace. The initial Discover check navigated directly to a query-string-selected tab; that rendered the tab but did not invoke the watcher that starts the registry request. I replaced it with the user-equivalent click from Docs and monitored the request through completion.

## Challenges and blockers

The key challenge was distinguishing rendered state from a successfully exercised state. A route can look populated even when an attempted fixture did not take effect, and a tab can render its content without having triggered its async loading action. Instrumenting requests and reproducing the user interaction resolved both uncertainties. There were no remaining blockers. The destructive or externally visible actions on the pages were not necessary to establish this review finding and remained unconfirmed.

## Key learnings

When verifying cached views, install the API interception before navigation and inspect whether the expected request actually matched. When async work is attached to a tab-change watcher, exercise the tab change instead of relying on a URL query to initiate it. Waiting alone does not establish completion; the response status and visible loaded data together provide stronger evidence. Both corrected checks passed without requiring source changes, and the deployment empty state and Discover completion are now recorded with the method that produced them.
